blocks.prompt: Four Shapes, One Animal
blocks.text: A butterfly does not grow the way you grow. It changes shape four times. First it is an egg, smaller than a grain of rice. The egg is stuck under a leaf. Then a caterpillar hatches out. Its first job is to eat. It eats leaves all day and gets bigger and bigger. Soon its skin is too tight, so it wriggles out of it. It does this about five times. Then the caterpillar hangs upside down and turns into a chrysalis. A chrysalis is a hard green case. Inside, the caterpillar is turning into something new. Two weeks later the case cracks open. A butterfly climbs out with wet, folded wings.

blocks.prompt: Four Animals in One Life
blocks.text: A butterfly lives its life as four different animals. Scientists call this complete metamorphosis. It begins as an egg, often no bigger than a pinhead, glued to the underside of a leaf. A monarch mom picks a milkweed leaf, because milkweed is the only thing her caterpillars can eat. Stage two is the caterpillar, and its whole job is eating. A monarch caterpillar can grow about two thousand times heavier in two weeks. Its skin cannot stretch that far, so it crawls out of its skin about five times, like taking off a shirt that got too small. Stage three is the chrysalis. The caterpillar hangs upside down in a J shape, wriggles out of its skin one last time, and underneath is a smooth green case with tiny gold dots. This is not a cocoon. Moths spin cocoons out of silk. A chrysalis is the caterpillar's own skin, gone hard. Stage four takes about two weeks to arrive. The case turns clear, you can see orange wings through it, and the butterfly pushes out. Its wings are crumpled and wet. It has to hang still and pump them full before it can fly.

blocks.prompt: The Insect That Rebuilds Itself
blocks.text: A caterpillar and a butterfly are the same animal. That sentence is easy to say and very hard to believe, because almost nothing about them matches. A caterpillar has chewing jaws; a butterfly has a drinking straw that coils under its head. A caterpillar crawls on stubby grippers; a butterfly has six legs and four scaled wings. They eat different food, live in different places, and could not swap jobs for a single day. The switch happens inside the chrysalis, and it is stranger than most people expect. The caterpillar does not simply sprout wings. Once the case hardens, the caterpillar releases enzymes that digest most of its own body. Muscle, gut, and skin break down into a thick soup of cells and nutrients. If you opened a chrysalis at the wrong moment, that is roughly what would pour out. What survives are small clusters called imaginal discs. The caterpillar has carried them since the day it hatched, folded away and unused, one disc for each future wing, leg, eye, and antenna. When the soup is ready, the discs feed on it and grow. The butterfly is built out of the melted caterpillar, like a sandcastle knocked flat and reshaped into a different castle from the same sand. Two weeks later the case splits. The butterfly that climbs out is crumpled and useless. It hangs upside down and pumps hemolymph, which is its blood, from its swollen belly into hollow veins in its wings until they stretch flat and harden. Only then can it fly. The animal that hatched from the egg to eat leaves has spent its whole short life building the animal that will drink nectar and lay the next batch of eggs.

blocks.prompt: The Soup That Remembers
blocks.text: Every butterfly is really two animals sharing one life, and they are built to never meet. The caterpillar chews leaves. The butterfly drinks nectar. The caterpillar cannot fly and the butterfly cannot bite. They do not compete for a single meal, which is exactly the point. Biologists think this division is a large part of why complete metamorphosis has been so successful: about four out of every five insect species on Earth now develop this way, beetles and bees and flies and ants included. The changeover is more extreme than that word suggests. When a monarch caterpillar has eaten enough, it spins a small silk button, hooks itself on, and hangs in a J. It molts one final time, and the skin underneath is not skin at all. It is a hard green case flecked with metallic gold: the chrysalis. This is where the confusion usually starts. A cocoon is a different thing. A cocoon is a silk bag that many moths spin around themselves from the outside. A chrysalis is the animal itself, hardened. Inside, the caterpillar releases digestive enzymes and dissolves. Most of its tissues break down into a nutrient soup. But the caterpillar was never only a caterpillar. Since the day it hatched it has carried imaginal discs, folded packets of cells that were doing nothing at all, one for each wing, each leg, each eye. The discs are not dissolved. They feed on the soup of the body that carried them, divide quickly, and assemble into an adult. Even the nervous system is not entirely erased. In one well known experiment, researchers taught tobacco hornworm caterpillars to avoid a particular smell by pairing it with a mild electric shock. Weeks later, after those caterpillars had liquefied and rebuilt themselves as moths, the moths still avoided that smell. Something survived the soup. When the adult is finished, the chrysalis turns transparent and the folded orange and black shows through. The butterfly splits the case, drags itself out, and is briefly helpless: its wings are wet crumpled bags. It hangs and pumps hemolymph, its blood, into the wing veins until they stretch tight and dry. An hour or two later, an animal that spent its childhood as a slow green tube of appetite lifts off and flies.

blocks.prompt: The Soup That Remembers: What Really Happens Inside a Chrysalis
blocks.text: A caterpillar is not a young butterfly in the way a puppy is a young dog. A puppy grows into its adult shape gradually, keeping the same legs, the same jaw, the same body plan, only larger. A caterpillar does something else entirely. It builds a butterfly out of itself, and it does not survive the process intact. Biologists call the strategy complete metamorphosis, and it has quietly conquered the planet: roughly four out of every five insect species, beetles and bees and flies and ants included, run their lives on the same four stage plan of egg, larva, pupa, adult. Consider what the two stages actually have in common, which is almost nothing. A monarch caterpillar has chewing mandibles and eats exactly one thing, milkweed, whose sap is toxic enough to sicken most animals and which the caterpillar stores in its own tissues as chemical armor. It crawls on three pairs of true legs and five pairs of fleshy prolegs. It cannot fly, cannot mate, and cannot travel much further than the next plant. The adult monarch has no mandibles at all. It has a proboscis, a coiled straw for nectar, feet that can taste a leaf, and four wings covered in overlapping scales. A female drums a leaf with her front legs to check that it really is milkweed before she lays. The adult can cross a continent. The larva exists to eat and grow; the adult exists to travel and reproduce. They do not compete for a single resource, and that separation is widely thought to be the engine behind this group's success. The handover happens in the chrysalis, and the details are stranger than the cartoon version. The caterpillar spins a silk button, hangs from it in a J, and molts one final time. Beneath that last shed skin is not more skin but a hardened case, jade green and flecked with metallic gold. This is worth getting right: a chrysalis is not a cocoon. A cocoon is a silk bag that many moths spin around themselves from the outside. A chrysalis is the insect's own hardened body wall, with the animal sealed inside it. Then the caterpillar digests itself. Enzymes flood its tissues, and muscle, gut, and fat break down into a thick nutrient broth. Cut a chrysalis open at the wrong moment and that is essentially what runs out. But the caterpillar was never merely a caterpillar. Since it was an embryo it has carried imaginal discs, small folded packets of cells held in reserve and doing no work at all: one for each wing, each leg, each eye, each antenna. The discs are not digested. They consume the broth of the body that carried them and grow into an adult. The butterfly is not an addition to the caterpillar. It is the caterpillar, rearranged. And something crosses the gap. In 2008, researchers at Georgetown University trained tobacco hornworm caterpillars to avoid the smell of ethyl acetate by pairing that odor with a mild electric shock. The caterpillars pupated, dissolved, and rebuilt themselves as moths. The adult moths still avoided the smell. A memory formed in a body that no longer exists was carried into a body that had not existed yet. The end of it is oddly fragile. The case turns clear, folded orange shows through, and the butterfly forces its way out soft and crumpled, its wings useless wet bags. It hangs upside down and pumps hemolymph, its blood, into hollow veins until the wings stretch flat and harden. If it falls, or if it cannot find room to hang, the wings set crooked and it will never fly. The animal spends two weeks as a green tube of appetite, liquefies itself completely, reassembles from spare parts, and then everything depends on whether it can hang still for an hour.
